planting.note: Divide or transplant in spring; shear hard in early summer to control sprawl.

directions: A heirloom pass-along selection traced to a South Carolina plantation garden, valued for its sprawling groundcover habit and lavender-purple daisies that open unusually late, often into November. Stems root as they spread, so give it room or an early-to-midsummer haircut to keep it in bounds. Thrives on neglect once established and draws heavy monarch and bee traffic during fall migration. Cut the whole clump to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges.

common_name: Dream of Beauty Aromatic Aster (Pink Aromatic Aster)

planting.note: Pinch or shear by about a quarter in early summer for a denser, more floriferous mound.

directions: A compact, low-mounding form of the native aromatic aster that stays well under a foot tall while smothering itself in clear pink, gold-centered flowers from late summer into fall. Handles sandy, clay, or average soils and shrugs off drought once rooted in, making it a dependable dry-border or edging choice. Deer and rabbits generally leave it alone, and the aromatic foliage is a bonus when brushed. Leave the seed heads standing for winter texture and cut back close to the crown in early spring.

common_name: Honeysong Pink New England Aster (Compact Pink New England Aster)

planting.note: Pinch stems back in early summer to reduce need for staking and encourage branching.

directions: A garden-bred selection of the native New England aster carrying clear pink, gold-centered blooms from late summer well into fall, sized for the middle to back of a border. Give it steady moisture and airflow between plants to discourage powdery mildew, and divide every few years to maintain vigor. Tall stems can flop in rich soil, so an early pinch or light staking keeps the display upright. A strong late-season nectar source for bees and migrating monarchs.

common_name: Billowing Pink Aromatic Aster (Chicagoland Grows Pink Aster)

planting.note: No pinching or staking required; give room for a wide mounding spread.

directions: Introduced through the Chicago Botanic Garden breeding program, this dense mounding aster covers itself in soft pink daisies for a long six-week stretch from late September into November. It self-supports without staking and shows strong resistance to rust and powdery mildew, holding up well in humid late-summer weather. Drought-tolerant once established and adaptable to a range of soils, it suits mass plantings, foundations, and pollinator borders alike. Cut back near the crown after the foliage browns in winter.
sources: Chicagoland Grows / Chicago Botanic Garden breeding program

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich woodland soil; spreads slowly by rhizome to form a groundcover colony.

directions: A naturally occurring hybrid between bigleaf aster and showy aster, grown chiefly for its bold, coarsely toothed heart-shaped foliage that carpets dry shade through the growing season. Flat-topped clusters of lavender-blue flowers appear in late summer atop the foliage mat, though bloom can be sparse in deeper shade. Mildew-resistant and deer-resistant, it slowly spreads by rhizome to knit together a durable woodland groundcover under trees. Best used where its leaf texture, rather than heavy flowering, is the main attraction.
